The disconfirming signal: if a meaningful share of blocked transactions are confirmed as genuine fraud attempts upon review, the rule is working as intended and the drop reflects real fraud being caught, not a calibration problem.

Immediate mitigation: raise the rule's threshold for this merchant category specifically, or temporarily exempt established repeat payers with clean histories, to reduce false positives while a proper recalibration is done. Durable fix: build category-specific fraud-rule thresholds informed by each category's normal transaction distribution, rather than one blanket rule across all merchant categories, and require a false-positive-rate check before any fraud-rule change ships broadly. Guardrail metric: false-positive rate (blocked-then-confirmed-legitimate transactions) tracked per rule and per merchant category, alerted whenever it exceeds a set tolerance, so a miscalibrated rule is caught before it meaningfully dents legitimate payment success.

pitfalls: Assuming any drop tied to a fraud rule is automatically 'working as intended' without checking the false-positive rate against confirmed fraud
Applying one blanket fraud-rule threshold across merchant categories with very different normal transaction patterns

cases.title: A CRED active-user 'drop' that turns out to be a metric definition change
cases.prompt: CRED's reported monthly active users fell 22% the same month the analytics team refreshed the definition of an 'active user.' Walk me through your root-cause analysis.
context: CRED is an Indian fintech app that rewards users for paying credit card bills on time and offers additional financial products.
CRED requires users to link and verify a credit card to access most of its core features.
CRED has expanded beyond credit card bill payments into products like short-term lending and a rewards/coin system.
assumptions: assumed: reported MAU fell 22% month-over-month, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the analytics team's definition refresh changed what counts as an 'active' session or action within the same month
assumed: no change was made to CRED's product, onboarding, or marketing spend that month
followUps: Once you suspect a definition change, what's the fastest way to prove the underlying usage didn't actually change?
How would you communicate a metric-definition-driven drop to a board or investor audience without it reading as a cover story?
What process would you put in place so a definition change never again looks indistinguishable from a real business decline?

stages.walkthrough: I'd confirm the metric is reported MAU, down 22% month-over-month, and that this decline coincides exactly with the month the analytics team refreshed the 'active user' definition rather than any product or marketing change. That coincidence, a metric-definition change landing in the same month as the reported drop, is the detail I'd flag as needing scrutiny before treating this as a real user decline.

I'd get the exact before-and-after definition of 'active': for instance, if the old definition counted any app open as active, and the new one requires a completed credit-related action (a bill payment, a card-linked transaction), that alone could produce a large apparent drop with zero change in real user behaviour. I'd recompute the prior month's MAU using the new definition retroactively; if the retroactive number is much closer to this month's reported number than the originally-reported prior-month number was, that's strong evidence the drop is definitional, not behavioural.

I'd segment the apparent decline by exactly which user actions moved from 'counted as active' to 'not counted as active' under the new definition. If nearly the entire 22-point gap is explained by users who opened the app or browsed rewards without completing a credit-related action -- precisely the behaviour the new definition excludes -- that confirms the drop is mechanical rather than a genuine falloff in engagement.

Framed as an internal cause even though it's not a real usage decline: the definition refresh itself is the direct cause of the reported number moving, specifically by narrowing which actions qualify a user as 'active' that month. I'd check whether the analytics team documented the rationale for the change (for example, wanting a definition more tied to financial engagement rather than passive app opens) and whether they retroactively restated prior months, since a restated baseline would have avoided this appearing as a cliff at all.

Given the precise alignment with a documented internal definition change and no concurrent product or marketing shift, an external cause is unlikely, but I'd still check underlying raw session counts and transaction volumes for that month to make sure a genuine external event (for example, a seasonal dip in discretionary card spend) isn't also contributing on top of the definitional effect.

Given a scenario where retroactively applying the new definition to the prior month produces a MAU figure within a couple of percentage points of this month's reported number, my leading hypothesis is that the 22-point drop is almost entirely explained by the definition change, not a real decline in engaged users. The confirming query: compare this month's MAU under the new definition against the prior month's MAU recomputed under the same new definition, rather than against the prior month's originally-reported number. The disconfirming signal: if a meaningful gap remains even after applying the new definition consistently to both months, some of the drop is real and needs its own investigation.

Immediate mitigation: republish the prior months' MAU restated under the new definition alongside this month's figure, so any stakeholder comparing month-over-month is comparing like-for-like rather than seeing a false cliff. Durable fix: establish a standing rule that any metric-definition change must be accompanied by a retroactive restatement of at least the trailing 6-12 months, published in the same update, so a definition change is never visually indistinguishable from a real business decline. Guardrail metric: a 'definition version' tag attached to every headline metric's historical series, so anyone reading a trend line can immediately see where a definition boundary falls.

pitfalls: Reporting a definition-driven drop as a headline business decline without checking whether a like-for-like restatement would close most of the gap
Assuming a metric-definition change and a business decline can't both be true and stopping the investigation as soon as the definition change is found

cases.title: Root-cause a slow DAU bleed on Dream11 in the off-season
cases.prompt: Dream11's DAU has been sliding roughly 3% a week for the past six weeks, with no single triggering event visible in release logs. Walk me through your root-cause analysis.
context: Dream11 is an Indian fantasy sports platform where users create teams and compete based on real-world match statistics, primarily cricket.
Dream11 usage has historically spiked sharply during major cricket tournaments such as the IPL and Cricket World Cup, and fallen off during periods with no major matches.
Dream11 has been a prominent sponsor closely associated with Indian cricket events and runs large marketing campaigns tied to tournament windows.
assumptions: assumed: DAU has declined approximately 3% week-over-week for six consecutive weeks, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: no major international or domestic cricket tournament has been running during this six-week window
assumed: no significant product release or marketing campaign change coincides with the start of the slide
followUps: How would you distinguish a normal seasonal bleed from an early warning sign of real product decay, if both look like a slow slide?
What would you want to see before concluding this is 'just the off-season' rather than investigating further?
How would you set a DAU goal for a team during a period you expect to be seasonally weak?

stages.walkthrough: I'd confirm the metric is overall DAU, declining roughly 3% week-over-week for six consecutive weeks, forming a steady slide rather than a sudden cliff, and confirm there's no single release or config change visible in the logs that lines up with when the slide began. A smooth, gradual decline with no discrete trigger point is itself an important clue, since it points away from a single internal or external event and toward something continuous, like a change in the underlying match calendar.

I'd check whether the DAU definition or counting logic changed at any point in this six-week window, and whether any bot- or test-account filtering was adjusted gradually rather than as one deploy. Given no release-log entry lines up with the start of the slide, and the decline looks smooth rather than stepped, I'd treat this as a real usage decline rather than a measurement issue.

I'd cut the decline by user tenure (new vs long-tenured users), by whether users are contest-entry-active or just app-opening, and by geography. If the decline is broad-based across nearly all user segments and geographies rather than isolated to one cohort or platform, that points toward something affecting the whole user base uniformly, which is the signature of an external, environment-wide cause rather than a localized product issue.

Given no release or config change lines up with the slide's start and the decline is broad-based, an internal cause seems unlikely, but I'd still check whether push-notification volume or in-app promotional intensity was quietly reduced over this period, either deliberately (a cost-saving measure) or as a side effect of a marketing budget cycle unrelated to any code release.

My leading external cause is straightforward seasonality: this six-week window likely falls between major cricket tournaments, a period historically associated with lower fantasy-sports engagement across the category, not just for Dream11. I'd check the cricket match calendar for this window and compare this six-week decline pattern against the equivalent off-season window from the prior year.

Given a scenario where the decline is broad-based across user segments and geographies, and the six-week window falls in a gap with no major domestic or international tournament, my leading hypothesis is that this is expected seasonal decay in the absence of high-interest cricket matches to build contests around. The confirming query: overlay this six-week DAU trend against the same calendar window from the prior year, checking whether the decline rate and shape closely match. The disconfirming signal: if this year's decline is meaningfully steeper than the same window last year, seasonality alone doesn't explain it and a real, additional cause needs investigating.

Immediate mitigation: increase engagement around smaller, lower-profile matches or other sports contests during this gap to partially offset the seasonal lull, rather than treating the off-season as a dead period. Durable fix: build a seasonally-adjusted DAU baseline and forecast, so future off-season periods are measured against an expected seasonal curve rather than a flat prior-week comparison that always looks alarming. Guardrail metric: DAU trend compared against the same calendar-period baseline from the prior year, so a genuinely abnormal decline (steeper than the historical seasonal pattern) is distinguishable from expected seasonality at a glance.

pitfalls: Panicking over a six-week slide without first checking the match calendar for an obvious seasonal explanation
Comparing DAU only to the prior week rather than to the same calendar window a year earlier, which is what actually reveals whether the decline is normal seasonality

cases.title: Root-cause a driver acceptance drop in Ola's auto-rickshaw category
cases.prompt: Ola's driver acceptance rate for auto-rickshaw rides in one city fell steadily by 11 percentage points over three weeks, while cab-category acceptance stayed flat. Walk me through your root-cause analysis.
context: Ola is an Indian ride-hailing platform offering cab and auto-rickshaw rides booked through a mobile app.
Ola operates multiple vehicle categories, including auto-rickshaws, cabs, and bikes, in different Indian cities.
Ola pays drivers based on a commission and incentive structure that it has adjusted at various points.
assumptions: assumed: auto-rickshaw driver acceptance rate in this city fell 11 percentage points over three weeks, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: a change to the auto-rickshaw driver commission or incentive structure took effect at the start of this three-week window
assumed: cab-category acceptance rate in the same city stayed within its normal range over the same period
followUps: Your leading hypothesis is a commission change specific to auto drivers. What's the fastest way to confirm that versus a coincidental cause?
How would you weigh a durable fix that costs Ola margin against a guardrail that just monitors the problem?
What would change about your analysis if bike-category acceptance had also dropped alongside auto?

stages.walkthrough: I'd confirm the metric is driver acceptance rate for the auto-rickshaw category specifically in this city, down 11 percentage points over three weeks in a steady slide rather than a single-day cliff, while the cab category in the same city held flat over the same period. A category-specific, gradually-widening gap rather than a sudden citywide drop is the shape that most directly points toward something specific to auto drivers' economics or experience.

I'd check whether the acceptance-rate calculation or offer-window definition changed for the auto category specifically during this window, and whether any driver-app logging change affected how auto-category offers are recorded differently from cab offers. Given cab-category logging is unaffected and shows no comparable movement, and the auto-category decline tracks smoothly rather than stepping at a logging-change date, I'd treat this as a real behavioural change among auto drivers.

I'd cut the decline by time of day, by trip distance, and by driver tenure within the auto-rickshaw category. If the decline is concentrated on shorter, lower-fare trips and among more experienced, higher-earning drivers who have alternatives, that points toward a change in the economics of accepting a ride becoming less worthwhile for exactly the trips and drivers with the most choice; if it's uniform across trip length and driver tenure, that would point toward something else, like a broader city-level supply issue.

Given the category-specific and driver-tenure-concentrated pattern, my leading internal cause is a change to the auto-rickshaw commission or incentive structure that took effect at the start of this window, making shorter or lower-fare trips less attractive to accept relative to before. I'd check whether Ola adjusted the commission percentage or removed a per-trip incentive specifically for the auto category in this city, and whether the timing lines up with the start of the slide.

I'd still check whether a local fuel-price change disproportionately affects auto-rickshaw driver economics (since autos typically run on CNG, with its own separate pricing dynamics from petrol/diesel used by cabs), or whether a competing platform launched an auto-specific driver incentive in this city during the same window, pulling supply away from Ola specifically for that category.

Given a scenario where the decline concentrates on shorter trips and among higher-tenure drivers, and a commission change for the auto category took effect right as the slide began, my leading hypothesis is that the new commission structure made shorter auto trips less economically worthwhile, so drivers with the most alternative options are declining them more often. The confirming query: compare acceptance rate for short-distance auto trips before and after the commission change date, isolated to this city, against acceptance rate for longer auto trips over the same period. The disconfirming signal: if short and long trips show a similar decline, the commission change on short-trip economics specifically isn't the driver and I'd look at the CNG pricing or competitor-incentive explanation instead.

Immediate mitigation: reintroduce a minimum-fare top-up or short-trip incentive for the auto category in this city to restore the economics of accepting shorter trips while a full commission review happens. Durable fix: redesign the commission structure to scale with trip economics rather than applying a flat percentage that disproportionately penalizes low-fare, short-distance trips, and pilot any future commission change in a small set of cities before a full rollout. Guardrail metric: acceptance rate segmented by trip-fare tier for each vehicle category, monitored continuously after any commission or incentive change, so a fare-tier-specific effect like this is caught within days rather than three weeks.

pitfalls: Treating a category-specific decline as a citywide supply problem instead of noticing that the unaffected category rules out a general city-level cause
Rolling out a commission change city-wide or nationally without a small pilot to catch a fare-tier-specific effect first

cases.title: Diagnose a flattened week-4 retention curve for Zerodha's new account cohort
cases.prompt: Zerodha's week-4 retention for new trading-account cohorts has flattened at a lower level for the last two months compared to the prior six months. As the PM for onboarding, how would you diagnose what changed and set a goal to recover it?
context: Zerodha is an Indian discount stock brokerage offering trading and investment accounts with no advisory fees.
Opening a Zerodha trading and demat account requires a KYC (know-your-customer) verification process before a user can place their first trade.
Zerodha's Kite platform is used for trading, while Coin is used for mutual fund investments.
assumptions: assumed: week-4 retention (placing at least one trade in week 4 after account activation) has flattened roughly 8 percentage points below the prior six-month average, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the KYC completion rate itself has stayed roughly stable over this period
assumed: no brokerage fee or account-opening cost change occurred during this window
followUps: How would you tell whether this is an activation problem (users never really got started) versus a habit problem (they started but didn't return)?
If your data showed the drop was entirely explained by a shift in acquisition channel mix, would you still call this a retention problem?
How would you set a goal here differently for the onboarding team versus the marketing/acquisition team?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume week-4 retention means placing at least one trade in the fourth week after account activation, that it's flattened about 8 percentage points below the prior six-month average for the last two months, and that KYC completion and fees have stayed stable over this window, so the cause is more likely downstream of account opening than at the gate itself. My plan: give brief product and business context, then spend most of the time building a metric framework that decomposes this curve into its likely components, and close with a goal for the onboarding team.

Zerodha's business model is volume-driven, low-cost brokerage, meaning revenue depends heavily on active traders generating brokerage and other transaction-linked fees rather than one-time account-opening revenue, so a durably lower week-4 retention directly threatens the business, not just an engagement vanity metric. Competitively, Zerodha's low-fee positioning has drawn a wave of new-to-investing users, especially since 2020, who differ meaningfully from earlier tech-savvy early adopters in how much guidance and hand-holding they need to place a confident first few trades. The mission connecting this to the company's purpose is 'make investing accessible without pushing people to trade more than they should,' which frames retention here as a proxy for genuine comfort with the platform, not just raw activity.

The ecosystem players are new account holders (value = a low-cost, self-directed way to invest), Zerodha (value = sustainable trading volume from a comfortable, returning user base), and the broader market/regulator (value = well-informed retail participation, which SEBI-aligned platforms are expected to support). To diagnose the flattening, I'd decompose week-4 retention into its upstream stages: KYC-to-first-trade conversion (already assumed stable), first-trade-to-week-2-return rate, and week-2-to-week-4 return rate, since a flat week-4 number could hide very different stories depending on where in that chain the actual softness lives. I'd also segment by acquisition channel and by whether the user's first trade was in equities directly or via a guided mutual-fund SIP through Coin, since a channel-mix shift toward less-informed, lower-intent users would show up as lower retention with no change to the product experience itself. If the softness concentrates in the first-trade-to-week-2 window specifically, and disproportionately in one newer acquisition channel, that points to an activation and education gap for that channel's users rather than a platform-wide problem; if it's spread evenly across channels and stages, that would point to something structural, like a broader retail risk-appetite shift in the market.

For the onboarding team, I'd set a goal on the first-trade-to-week-2 return rate specifically for the newer acquisition channel identified as the weak point, rather than on week-4 retention directly, since that's the stage closest to what onboarding actually controls. I'd target recovering roughly half the flattening gap within one quarter, defended by the size of that channel's share of new accounts and by the assumption that a guided first-trade education flow (comparable to what already exists for Coin's SIP onboarding) can close a meaningful share of the gap based on how much stronger Coin's own early retention has historically been. This bridges strategy to execution because the onboarding team can directly ship a channel-specific first-week education flow and measure its effect on that one stage within weeks, while a stable KYC completion rate and overall trading-volume guardrail ensure the fix isn't just accelerating account openings without actually building trading comfort.

pitfalls: Treating 'week-4 retention' as one number to fix directly instead of decomposing which upstream stage of the funnel actually softened
Assuming the cause must be a product regression without first checking whether a shift in acquisition channel mix changed the composition of who's in the cohort

cases.title: Diagnose a diluted 30-day retention curve after Meesho's paid-acquisition push
cases.prompt: Meesho's 30-day retention for its monthly new-shopper cohort dropped noticeably the month a large paid-acquisition campaign ran. As the retention PM, how would you diagnose this and set a goal for the next quarter?
context: Meesho is an Indian e-commerce platform, originally built around social commerce and reselling, now operating as a broader online marketplace.
Meesho has offered zero-commission listings for sellers at various points as part of its growth strategy.
Meesho runs paid marketing and referral-driven acquisition campaigns to grow its user base.
assumptions: assumed: 30-day retention for the campaign-month cohort fell roughly 10 percentage points versus the prior month's organic-heavy cohort, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the paid campaign roughly doubled new-shopper volume for that one month
assumed: no major product or app change shipped during the same month
followUps: How would you separate 'this channel brings lower-quality users' from 'this channel brings the same users but the onboarding didn't fit them'?
If the paid channel is genuinely lower-retention but much cheaper per acquisition, how would you decide whether to keep running it?
What would make you recommend pausing the campaign entirely versus just adjusting onboarding?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the campaign-month cohort's 30-day retention fell about 10 percentage points versus the prior organic-heavy month, that the campaign roughly doubled new-shopper volume that month, and that no product change shipped alongside it, so a channel-driven composition shift is my starting suspicion. My plan: briefly frame the business context, then build a metric framework that separates channel effects from genuine product effects, and close with a goal that reflects what I find.

Meesho's model depends on high-volume, low-margin transactions across a broad, often first-time-online-shopper base, so new-user growth quality matters as much as raw volume: an acquisition channel that brings shoppers who never complete a first purchase or churn immediately adds cost without building the repeat-order behaviour the marketplace depends on. Competitively, Meesho differentiates on price and accessibility for value-conscious shoppers, many new to online shopping altogether, which means channel-driven shifts in who's arriving can meaningfully change the base rate of retention even with zero product change. The mission this connects to is building lasting trust with first-time online shoppers, which a purely volume-driven acquisition push can work against if it isn't matched with onboarding suited to less experienced users.

The ecosystem players are new shoppers (value = an accessible, trustworthy first online-shopping experience), sellers (value = a growing, returning buyer base), and Meesho (value = sustainable repeat-order volume rather than one-time transactions). To diagnose the drop, I'd first check whether retention differs by acquisition source within that same month's cohort -- comparing paid-campaign-sourced shoppers against the organic and referral-sourced shoppers who arrived in the same month -- since if the paid segment alone shows the drop while organic and referral segments hold steady, this is a channel-composition effect diluting the blended average, not a platform-wide retention problem. I'd also check first-order completion rate and first-order category for the paid segment specifically, since a channel that brings shoppers via a broad, low-intent ad (versus a targeted referral from someone who already trusts the platform) may simply attract people less ready to become repeat buyers. If instead the drop shows up evenly across paid and organic shoppers in that same month, that would point to something else changing platform-wide that month, not the campaign itself.

Assuming the diagnosis confirms the drop is concentrated in the paid-campaign segment, I'd set a goal for the growth/onboarding team on 30-day retention specifically for that acquisition channel, not on the blended platform-wide number, since blending would let true organic performance mask a real channel-quality problem. I'd target closing roughly half the gap between paid-channel and organic-channel retention within the next quarter, defended by testing a channel-specific onboarding flow (e.g., a more guided first-purchase experience with trust signals suited to less experienced shoppers) similar to lifts seen from onboarding changes in other price-sensitive, high-volume marketplaces. This bridges strategy to execution because the team can directly test and measure onboarding changes against this one channel's cohort, while a blended, platform-wide 30-day retention guardrail ensures the fix doesn't come at the expense of the already-healthy organic and referral cohorts.

pitfalls: Reading a blended retention drop as a platform-wide problem without first checking whether it's concentrated in the newly-scaled acquisition channel
Assuming a lower-retention paid channel is automatically not worth running, without weighing its retention against its cost per acquisition

cases.title: Diagnose a week-2 retention drop for a new Rapido rider cohort
cases.prompt: Week-2 retention for riders acquired through Rapido's latest referral campaign is running well below the retention of riders acquired through other channels in the same period. As the growth PM, how would you diagnose this and set a goal?
context: Rapido is an Indian bike-taxi and ride-hailing platform operating in multiple Indian cities.
Rapido shows riders an estimated fare, which can include surge pricing during high-demand periods, before they confirm a booking.
Rapido has expanded beyond bike taxis into auto-rickshaw and cab categories in some cities.
assumptions: assumed: week-2 retention for the referral-campaign cohort is roughly 12 percentage points below other channels' cohorts from the same period, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the referral campaign offered a first-ride discount to new riders
assumed: surge-pricing frequency was similar across cities for both the referral cohort and the comparison cohort
followUps: How would you separate 'the discount attracted one-time deal-seekers' from 'the first-ride experience itself was worse for this cohort'?
If the referred riders' first rides disproportionately hit surge pricing, how would that change your read of this data?
How would you design a referral incentive that's less likely to attract one-time-only users in the first place?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the referral cohort's week-2 retention runs about 12 percentage points below other channels in the same period, that the campaign offered a first-ride discount, and that surge-pricing exposure was similar across cohorts, so a pricing-experience difference isn't my starting suspicion. My plan: cover the product context briefly, then build a metric framework isolating whether this is a discount-driven quality issue or a genuine first-ride experience issue, and close with a goal for the referral program.

Rapido's business depends on riders forming a low-cost, convenient habit for short urban trips, competing against both other ride-hailing options and simply walking or using public transit for very short distances, so a new rider's first couple of rides are disproportionately important for establishing that habit before they default back to an alternative. Referral programs are a common low-cost-per-acquisition growth lever, but they inherently risk attracting people motivated primarily by the one-time discount rather than an ongoing need. The mission this connects to is building an everyday, trusted alternative to short-distance travel, which a discount-driven referral spike can undermine if the resulting riders were never going to become habitual users regardless of the actual ride experience.

The ecosystem players are new riders (value = an affordable, quick first-ride experience worth repeating), referring existing riders (value = a reward for a successful referral), and Rapido (value = a low-cost acquisition channel that still produces habitual riders, not just one-time discount users). To diagnose the gap, I'd first check whether the referral cohort's second-ride rate (did they even take a ride beyond the discounted first one) differs meaningfully from other channels, since if most of the retention gap is explained by riders never returning after the discounted ride specifically, that points to discount-seeking behaviour rather than a bad experience. I'd also check first-ride completion quality for the referral cohort specifically (driver wait time, ride cancellation rate, fare accuracy versus the shown estimate) compared to other channels' first rides, since if the referral cohort's first-ride experience was measurably worse, the gap could instead be a genuine service-quality issue concentrated on new riders in whichever cities or times referral campaigns were heaviest.

Assuming the diagnosis shows the gap is concentrated in riders who never took a second ride at all, rather than a worse first-ride experience, I'd set a goal for the growth team on second-ride conversion within 14 days specifically for referral-acquired riders, not on raw referral volume. I'd target closing a defined share of the gap versus other channels next quarter, defended by testing a smaller first-ride discount paired with a second-ride incentive instead of a single large first-ride-only discount, reasoning that spreading the incentive across the first two rides gives riders a reason to return before the campaign's cost-efficiency advantage over other channels is judged solely on volume. This bridges strategy to execution because the growth team directly controls the referral incentive structure, while an overall cost-per-retained-rider guardrail (not just cost-per-signup) ensures the referral program isn't optimized to look cheap on paper while producing riders who never really stick.

pitfalls: Judging a referral channel purely on cost-per-signup without checking whether its second-ride conversion is meaningfully worse than other channels
Assuming a lower-retention referral cohort means the ride experience was bad, without first checking whether they simply never returned after redeeming the one-time discount

cases.title: Diagnose a flattened repeat-purchase curve for Nykaa's loyalty cohort
cases.prompt: Nykaa's month-2 repeat-purchase rate for a recent new-customer cohort flattened at a lower level than the prior four cohorts. As the retention PM, how would you diagnose the cause and set a goal to recover it?
context: Nykaa is an Indian beauty and personal care e-commerce platform that also operates physical retail stores.
Nykaa sells both third-party brands and its own private-label beauty products.
Nykaa listed on Indian stock exchanges in 2021.
assumptions: assumed: month-2 repeat-purchase rate for this cohort is roughly 7 percentage points below the average of the prior four cohorts, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the cohort's first-purchase basket composition (mix of categories bought) is similar to prior cohorts
assumed: no sitewide pricing or shipping-fee change occurred during this cohort's first two months
followUps: How would you distinguish an assortment/stock-availability problem from a genuine shift in what this cohort wants to buy?
If the flattening were concentrated only in customers whose first purchase was a specific product category, how would that change your investigation?
How would you set a goal here differently for a merchandising/inventory team versus a lifecycle-marketing team?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume month-2 repeat-purchase rate for this cohort sits about 7 percentage points below the trailing four-cohort average, that first-purchase basket composition looks similar to prior cohorts, and that no sitewide pricing or shipping change happened during this window, so my starting suspicion is something more specific, like assortment or stock availability for repeat-purchase items. My plan: briefly frame Nykaa's business context, build a metric framework to isolate where in the repeat-purchase journey the flattening lives, and close with a goal split across the teams that could act on it.

Nykaa's business model depends heavily on repeat purchases of consumable beauty products (skincare, makeup that gets used up and repurchased), so a flattened month-2 repeat-purchase curve directly threatens lifetime value, not just an engagement metric. Its private-label and exclusive-brand assortment is a key competitive differentiator against generic e-commerce marketplaces, meaning assortment health (in-stock rates on frequently-repurchased items) matters more for Nykaa's retention than for a platform selling interchangeable commodity goods. The mission this connects to is being the trusted, go-to destination for a customer's ongoing beauty routine, which depends on customers being able to reliably reorder what they already love.

The ecosystem players are customers (value = reliably being able to reorder trusted products), brand partners including Nykaa's own private labels (value = a growing base of repeat buyers), and Nykaa (value = high customer lifetime value driven by repeat, not one-time, purchases). To diagnose the flattening, I'd first check repeat-purchase rate specifically for customers whose first purchase included a product that later went out of stock or was discontinued during their second-month window, since a stock-availability problem on frequently-repurchased items would show up precisely as a lower repeat rate concentrated in exactly that customer subset, with the rest of the cohort behaving normally. I'd also check whether this cohort's first-purchase products skew toward a category with historically lower repurchase cadence (for instance, a one-time gifting item versus a regular skincare consumable), which would look like a retention problem but actually reflect a natural, expected difference in category-level repurchase timing. If the flattening is spread evenly across all product categories and stock-availability is unaffected, that would point toward something broader, like a lifecycle-marketing or reminder-email change that stopped reaching this cohort effectively.

Assuming the diagnosis shows the flattening concentrates on customers whose repurchase-relevant product went out of stock, I'd set a goal jointly owned by merchandising/inventory and lifecycle marketing: an in-stock rate target for the top repeat-purchase-driving SKUs, alongside a month-2 repeat-purchase-rate recovery target for customers affected by that stockout. I'd target recovering the majority of the 7-point gap within a quarter, defended by the size of the affected SKU's contribution to this cohort's first-purchase basket and by the assumption that restocking plus a targeted reminder to affected customers once the item is back can recapture most of the lapsed repeat-purchase intent. This bridges strategy to execution because inventory directly controls the stock-availability lever while lifecycle marketing directly controls re-engaging the affected customers, and an overall repeat-purchase-rate guardrail across all cohorts ensures this fix doesn't just move the problem to a different cohort or category.

pitfalls: Assuming a flattened repeat-purchase curve is a marketing or engagement problem before checking whether a specific frequently-repurchased product simply went out of stock
Comparing repeat-purchase rate across cohorts without accounting for a shift in first-purchase category mix that naturally has a different repurchase cadence

cases.title: Diagnose a week-4 retention gap for Blinkit's newly launched cities
cases.prompt: Week-4 retention for new users acquired in Blinkit's recently launched tier-2 cities is running well below retention for equivalent new-user cohorts in its established metro markets. As the PM for new-market expansion, how would you diagnose this and set a goal?
context: Blinkit (formerly Grofers) is an Indian quick-commerce grocery delivery platform promising delivery within minutes from local dark stores.
Blinkit was acquired by Zomato (now Eternal) in 2022.
Blinkit competes with other quick-commerce players such as Zepto and Swiggy Instamart in Indian cities.
assumptions: assumed: week-4 retention for new-city cohorts runs roughly 15 percentage points below equivalent-tenure cohorts in established metros, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: these new tier-2 cities launched with fewer dark stores per capita than the established metros had at the same point in their own launch history
assumed: delivery promise time (minutes) shown to users is the same nationally regardless of actual local fulfillment capacity
followUps: How would you tell whether this is a delivery-experience problem versus these cities simply having lower category fit for quick-commerce overall?
If dark-store density is the driver, would you recommend slowing new-city launches or accepting lower retention as a temporary cost of expansion?
How would you set a goal here that doesn't unfairly penalize a new-market team for a structural, not execution, gap?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume week-4 retention for new tier-2 city cohorts runs about 15 percentage points below equivalent-tenure metro cohorts, that these cities launched with lower dark-store density per capita than metros had at a comparable stage, and that the delivery-time promise shown to users doesn't yet adjust for local fulfillment capacity. My plan: frame the business context briefly, build a metric framework that isolates whether this is a delivery-experience gap tied to density, a genuine category-fit gap, or something else, and close with a goal appropriately split between expansion and operations teams.

Blinkit's entire value proposition rests on a specific, fast delivery-time promise, which is only achievable when dark-store density is high enough relative to local demand; expanding into new cities before that density is built is a deliberate growth trade-off, not a mistake, but it does mean new cities structurally start below the experience level that established metros offer. Competitively, all major quick-commerce players race for density and coverage in new cities simultaneously, so a slower, more cautious density build-out risks ceding early-mover advantage to a competitor. The mission this connects to is making minutes-fast delivery a reliable everyday habit, which depends on the delivery promise actually being met, not just advertised, in every city Blinkit operates in.

The ecosystem players are new-city customers (value = the same fast, reliable delivery promise as any metro customer), dark-store operations teams (value = enough local demand to justify the store's cost), and Blinkit (value = sustainable growth into new markets without diluting its core promise). To diagnose the gap, I'd check actual delivered time versus the promised time for orders in these new cities compared to metros, since if new-city orders are taking meaningfully longer than what's shown to the user at checkout, that's a direct, measurable trust-breaking gap rather than a vague 'new market adjustment' story. I'd also segment retention by distance from the nearest dark store within these cities, since if retention is meaningfully better for users living close to a store and meaningfully worse for those farther away, that isolates density (a fixable, ops-side variable) as the driver rather than these cities simply having lower underlying demand for quick-commerce as a category. If retention were uniformly low regardless of proximity to a dark store, that would instead suggest a category-fit issue -- these markets may just have different shopping habits -- which calls for a different response than building more stores.

Assuming the diagnosis confirms retention correlates strongly with proximity to a dark store, I'd set a goal jointly owned by operations and new-market expansion: a dark-store-density target (stores per capita, or percentage of new-city population within a set delivery-time radius) to reach within two quarters, paired with a week-4 retention target for new cohorts once that density threshold is hit in a given city, rather than expecting current cohorts to close the full gap immediately. I'd defend the density target's size by benchmarking against the density level established metros had reached by the point their own retention matched today's metro baseline. This bridges strategy to execution because operations directly controls store rollout pace, while new-market expansion controls launch sequencing and can choose to delay full-scale user acquisition marketing in a city until density catches up, and an actual-versus-promised delivery-time guardrail ensures the promise isn't overstated to new-city users in the meantime.

pitfalls: Treating lower retention in new cities as an onboarding or marketing problem without checking whether the actual delivery promise is being met there
Setting the same retention target for new and established cities without accounting for the structural density gap driving the difference

cases.title: Diagnose a week-4 retention drop explained by referral-incentive composition on Groww
cases.prompt: Week-4 retention for a recent new-investor cohort on Groww came in well below the trailing average, the same month a large one-time referral bonus campaign ran. As the PM for activation, how would you diagnose this and set a goal for the next quarter?
context: Groww is an Indian investment platform offering mutual funds, stocks, and other investment products through a mobile app.
Opening a Groww account requires KYC verification before a user can begin investing.
Groww has grown its user base partly through referral programs and low-cost, no-brokerage positioning.
assumptions: assumed: week-4 retention (defined as any app open with a portfolio view or new investment action) fell roughly 13 percentage points below the trailing six-month average for this cohort, as posed by the interviewer
assumed: the referral campaign offered a fixed cash bonus to both referrer and referee once the referee completed a small minimum first investment
assumed: KYC completion and first-investment completion rates for this cohort were similar to prior cohorts
followUps: How would you prove the drop is about who the campaign attracted rather than a genuine product issue that happened to coincide with it?
Would you recommend Groww run this kind of referral campaign again? What would you change about its design?
How would you set an activation-team goal without unfairly holding them accountable for a growth-team acquisition decision?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume week-4 retention for this cohort fell about 13 percentage points below the trailing six-month average, that the referral campaign paid both sides a fixed cash bonus once the referee made a small minimum first investment, and that KYC and first-investment completion rates for this cohort looked normal, meaning the funnel up to first investment wasn't the problem. My plan: frame the business and mission context, build a metric framework that tests whether this is a cohort-composition effect from the incentive design versus a genuine activation problem, and close with a goal appropriately scoped to the activation team.

Groww's business model depends on investors continuing to invest over time, since revenue is tied to ongoing transaction and asset-under-management activity, not a one-time account opening, so a cohort that invests once to claim a bonus and then disengages is close to worthless from a lifetime-value standpoint even though it looks identical to a genuine new investor in top-of-funnel metrics. Competitively, referral-driven growth is a common low-CAC lever across Indian fintech, but a bonus structured around a small minimum investment specifically risks attracting people optimizing for the reward rather than genuinely starting an investing habit. The mission this connects to is helping first-time investors build a lasting investing habit, which a reward-chasing cohort can directly undermine if the incentive isn't designed to select for genuine intent.

The ecosystem players are new investors (value = an easy, low-friction way to start investing), referring existing users (value = a cash reward for a successful referral), and Groww (value = a growing base of investors who keep transacting, not one-time bonus claimants). To diagnose the drop, I'd first check the size and nature of this cohort's first investment: if a large share of the campaign's new investors put in exactly the minimum qualifying amount and never added to it, that's a strong signal the incentive selected for bonus-chasers rather than genuine first-time investors, distinct from Groww's typical organic and non-incentivized-referral cohorts. I'd also compare week-4 retention for this cohort's minimum-investment sub-segment against the sub-segment that invested meaningfully more than the minimum, since if the higher-investment sub-segment's retention looks normal while the minimum-investment sub-segment's retention has cratered, that isolates the incentive's design, not a broader product issue, as the driver. If retention were uniformly low regardless of first-investment size, that would instead point toward a genuine activation-experience problem that happened to coincide with the campaign timing, not the campaign itself.

Assuming the diagnosis confirms the drop concentrates in the minimum-investment, bonus-chasing sub-segment, I'd set a goal jointly with the growth team on future referral-campaign design rather than asking activation to fix retention for a cohort that was never going to convert as designed: specifically, redesigning the incentive to require a meaningfully higher minimum investment, or to pay out the bonus in installments tied to continued activity over the first month. For the activation team specifically, I'd set a goal on week-4 retention excluding future bonus-driven minimum-investment cohorts, protecting the metric from being diluted by acquisition-design choices outside activation's control, while defending the incentive-redesign recommendation with the clear gap shown between the minimum-investment and higher-investment sub-segments in this campaign. This bridges strategy to execution because growth directly controls campaign incentive structure going forward, while activation can be fairly held accountable only for the retention of users it actually has a chance to influence.

pitfalls: Holding the activation team accountable for a retention drop that's actually explained by an acquisition-incentive design decision made by a different team
Assuming all referral-driven users behave the same way without splitting by whether they invested exactly the minimum qualifying amount or genuinely more

cases.title: Weigh engagement against well-being for Instagram's time-spent features
cases.prompt: Instagram has shipped features like 'You're all caught up' (marking when a user has seen all new posts) alongside features that encourage continued browsing, like Explore and Reels autoplay. How would you think about the trade-off between time-spent and user well-being when deciding what to build next?
context: Instagram has shipped 'You're all caught up' notices in the main feed, marking the point where a user has seen all new posts since their last visit.
Instagram also has features designed to extend session time, including an algorithmically ranked Explore tab and autoplaying Reels.
Meta has publicly discussed well-being-oriented features across its apps, including time-spent dashboards and reminder-to-take-a-break prompts.
assumptions: assumed: advertising revenue is meaningfully correlated with time spent in the near term, creating real business pressure toward engagement-maximizing features
assumed: a meaningful share of users report, in surveys or public sentiment, wanting more control over how much time they spend on the app
followUps: How would you decide whether a proposed feature belongs on the engagement side or the well-being side before building it?
If a well-being feature reduces session time but user satisfaction scores rise, how would you defend keeping it to a revenue-focused stakeholder?
How would you tell if 'time well spent' is actually happening, versus just less time spent?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume near-term ad revenue correlates with time spent, creating real pressure toward engagement features, while a meaningful user segment also wants more control over their usage. Plan: frame why this is a genuine trade-off and not a false one, define the ecosystem and competing metrics, then propose how to actually decide between the two.

Instagram's business model is advertising, which historically rewards more time spent and more content viewed, but Instagram's long-term license to operate depends on users continuing to trust and want to use the product, and a reputation for being addictive or harmful to well-being is a real long-term brand and regulatory risk. This makes the trade-off genuinely strategic, not just a product nice-to-have: optimizing purely for short-term time-spent metrics can undermine the long-term user trust the business depends on.

Ecosystem players: the user (value = a mix of connection, entertainment, and control over their own time), advertisers (value = attention and ad impressions), and Instagram (value = both near-term ad revenue and long-term platform trust). A pure time-spent North Star would systematically favor engagement features and starve well-being investment, so I'd argue for a composite North Star like 'sessions rated positively in exit surveys' or a satisfaction-weighted engagement metric, paired with guardrails on both sides: minimum ad-revenue-per-user (protecting the business) and a well-being signal like self-reported control-over-usage or voluntary use of time-limit tools (protecting the user). Implementable metrics: session length, session frequency, exit-survey sentiment score, and adoption/retention of well-being tools like 'You're all caught up' or break reminders, all trackable from existing event logs and periodic survey instrumentation. Any single feature proposal should be evaluated against both sides of this composite metric before shipping, not against time-spent alone.

For a well-being-focused feature team, I'd set a goal on adoption and voluntary continued use of a specific well-being tool (e.g., week-4 retention of users who enable break reminders) rather than a company-wide time-spent or revenue goal, since that's what the team actually controls and it's a genuine leading indicator of whether the feature is valued rather than ignored. I'd defend this goal to a revenue-focused stakeholder by tying it to the long-term trust guardrail: a user who trusts the platform to respect their time is a more durable long-term asset than marginal extra minutes today, and I'd propose measuring the net revenue effect over two to three quarters, not the first month, before judging the trade-off's true cost.

pitfalls: Treating time-spent and well-being as a zero-sum choice on every single feature, rather than recognizing some features can improve both
Judging a well-being feature's business cost only in the first month, before its long-term trust effect has had time to show up

cases.title: Weigh GMV growth against take-rate for Uber's driver incentive structure
cases.prompt: Uber can grow gross bookings (GMV) by subsidizing driver incentives, which lowers Uber's effective take-rate (its share of each fare) in the near term. How would you think about the trade-off between GMV growth and take-rate?
context: Uber reports both Gross Bookings (the total value of rides and deliveries transacted on its platform) and its take-rate (the share of gross bookings retained as revenue) in public financial disclosures.

Ride-hailing platforms commonly use driver incentives (bonuses for completing a set number of trips, surge-related earnings guarantees) to influence driver supply, especially in specific markets or time periods.
Uber operates in a competitive market with other ride-hailing platforms in most major geographies.
assumptions: assumed: driver supply (number of active drivers and their online hours) directly affects rider wait times and trip completion rates in a given market
assumed: take-rate reductions from incentives are a near-term, adjustable lever rather than a permanent structural change to Uber's revenue share
followUps: How would you decide which specific markets or time windows deserve incentive spend versus which don't?
If a competitor is aggressively subsidizing drivers in one city, how does that change your recommendation?
How would you know if incentive spend is actually growing the market versus just shifting drivers from a competitor at a cost that won't sustain itself?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume driver supply directly affects rider experience (wait time, completion rate) in a given market, and that take-rate reductions from incentives are an adjustable near-term lever, not permanent. Plan: frame the ecosystem and why this is a real trade-off, define the metrics on both sides, then propose how to decide when incentive spend is worth the take-rate cost.

Uber's marketplace depends on having enough driver supply to keep wait times low and trip completion high, since a rider who can't get a ride quickly will simply use a competitor; but Uber's own profitability and investor expectations depend on take-rate, its actual revenue share of each transaction. This makes incentive spend a genuine two-sided investment decision: it can grow the market (more GMV, more riders retained by good service) or simply give away margin without changing the underlying supply-demand balance, depending on the specific market's competitive dynamics.

Ecosystem players: riders (value = short wait times and reliable availability), drivers (value = predictable earnings), and Uber (value = sustainable revenue at scale). A GMV-only North Star would justify unlimited incentive spend regardless of profitability, while a take-rate-only North Star would starve driver supply in competitive markets and directly hurt the rider experience — so I'd propose a market-level 'contribution margin per trip after incentives' as the core decision metric, since it's implementable from existing trip and payout data and captures both sides jointly, paired with guardrails on rider wait time and trip completion rate (protecting the marketplace's basic function) and driver retention (protecting supply from eroding after an incentive program ends). Incentive spend should be evaluated market-by-market against this contribution margin, not as a single global lever, since competitive intensity and supply tightness vary a great deal by city.

For a marketplace-balance team, I'd set a quarterly goal on improving contribution-margin-per-trip in a defined set of currently-negative-margin markets, rather than a blanket GMV or take-rate target, since that's the metric that actually reflects whether incentive spend in those specific markets is working. I'd defend prioritizing certain markets over an across-the-board GMV push by showing which markets have the clearest driver-supply constraint (via wait-time and completion-rate data) versus which are already well-supplied and would just be giving away margin for no marketplace benefit.

pitfalls: Treating incentive spend as a single global lever instead of evaluating it market-by-market against actual supply constraints
Optimizing take-rate in a supply-constrained market without checking the resulting hit to rider wait time and trip completion

cases.title: Weigh host-supply growth against quality for Airbnb's Superhost program
cases.prompt: Airbnb's Superhost program sets a quality bar (response rate, review score, cancellation rate) that hosts must meet to earn the badge and its associated visibility boost. How would you think about the trade-off between keeping that bar strict (favoring quality) versus loosening it to grow the number of qualifying hosts (favoring supply)?
context: Airbnb's Superhost program awards a badge to hosts who meet criteria including a minimum number of completed stays, a high overall rating, a low cancellation rate, and a high response rate, reviewed quarterly.
Superhost listings have historically received additional visibility and discovery benefits in Airbnb's search and browsing experience.
Airbnb operates as a two-sided marketplace connecting hosts (supply) with guests (demand) across a large number of geographic markets that vary in listing density.
assumptions: assumed: Superhost-badge visibility meaningfully affects a listing's booking rate, based on how the program is positioned as a discovery benefit
assumed: the quality criteria (rating, cancellation rate, response rate) are reasonably correlated with actual guest experience quality
followUps: How would you evaluate whether loosening the bar in a specific under-supplied market is different from loosening it globally?
If Superhost qualification rates differ significantly between new and experienced hosts, how does that affect your recommendation?
How would you check whether the visibility boost is actually necessary to reward quality, versus quality already being self-reinforcing through guest reviews alone?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume the Superhost badge meaningfully affects booking rate through added visibility, and that its quality criteria are reasonably correlated with real guest experience. Plan: frame why this is a genuine two-sided trade-off, define the ecosystem and metrics, then propose a market-differentiated approach rather than a single global answer.

Airbnb's marketplace depends on both enough listing supply for guests to find a good option in their desired location and dates, and high enough quality that guests trust booking a stranger's home sight-unseen; the Superhost program is explicitly designed to reward the second while implicitly gating some of the visibility that drives the first. This makes the strictness of the bar a genuine strategic lever: too strict in a thin market starves supply visibility where it's needed most, too loose anywhere risks diluting the trust signal that makes the badge meaningful to guests.

Ecosystem players: guests (value = confidence they're booking a reliable, good-quality stay), hosts (value = visibility and booking volume as a reward for quality), and Airbnb (value = overall marketplace trust and booking volume). A pure qualifying-host-count North Star would push toward loosening the bar everywhere, eroding the badge's meaning to guests, while a pure guest-satisfaction-score North Star ignores that thin markets need supply first. I'd propose evaluating markets separately on listing density (a proxy for supply thinness) and on Superhost-badge booking-rate lift (from existing booking and badge data), keeping the bar strict in well-supplied markets where quality differentiation matters most to guests, and only considering a modestly adjusted bar in genuinely thin markets, guardrailed by guest review scores for newly-qualifying hosts under any adjusted criteria (making sure a loosened bar doesn't quietly admit lower-quality hosts) and by badge booking-rate lift holding steady (confirming the badge still means something to guests).

For the host-quality team, I'd set a goal specific to under-supplied markets: raise the Superhost qualification rate in a defined list of thin markets by a set percentage this quarter through host coaching and support rather than criteria loosening, since coaching addresses the actual gap (hosts not yet meeting the bar) without touching the bar's meaning everywhere else. Guest review scores for newly-qualifying hosts in those markets stay a hard guardrail owned jointly with the trust and safety team, so growth in badge count doesn't quietly come at the cost of guest trust.

pitfalls: Loosening the Superhost bar globally to solve what is actually a market-specific supply problem in a handful of thin geographies
Growing badge count without checking that newly-qualifying hosts under any adjusted criteria are actually delivering the same guest experience

cases.title: Weigh meaningful interactions against raw engagement for a social feed ranking change
cases.prompt: In 2018, Facebook publicly announced a News Feed ranking change to prioritize 'meaningful social interactions' between friends and family over passive content consumption, stating this could reduce time spent in the short term. How would you think about this kind of trade-off between a narrower quality-of-interaction metric and raw engagement?
context: Facebook publicly announced in January 2018 a News Feed algorithm change prioritizing posts that generate conversation and meaningful interaction between people, over public content from businesses, brands, and media.
Facebook's public statement at the time said this change was expected to reduce the total time people spend on Facebook in the near term.
Facebook's business model is advertising, which is affected by both total time spent and the volume/quality of content shown.
assumptions: assumed: 'meaningful social interaction' can be operationalized via signals like commenting, sharing to a friend, or engaging in back-and-forth conversation on a post, distinct from passive scrolling or a like
assumed: a short-term reduction in time spent following the change was an accepted, anticipated cost at the time, based on the public framing
followUps: How would you defend accepting a near-term time-spent decline to a stakeholder focused on quarterly ad revenue?
How would you distinguish a 'meaningful interaction' from an engagement-bait comment thread that isn't actually meaningful?
What would you want to see in the data a few quarters later to confirm the trade-off was worth it?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume meaningful interaction can be operationalized via signals like commenting and back-and-forth conversation distinct from passive scrolling, and that a near-term time-spent decline was an accepted, anticipated cost of this change. Plan: frame why the company made this trade-off deliberately, define the ecosystem and competing metrics, then propose how you'd defend and measure it.

Facebook's long-term value to users depends on feeling that time on the platform is genuinely valuable for staying connected to people they care about, not just a source of passive, low-value content consumption; if users come to feel their feed is mostly low-value, they may reduce usage far more severely over the long term than any near-term optimization would predict. The public framing of this change suggests the company judged long-term platform health and user trust to be worth more than short-term engagement, which is exactly the kind of trade-off a raw engagement-only North Star can't see, since it only measures the thing being deliberately, strategically reduced.

Ecosystem players: individual users (value = genuine connection with people they know), publishers and brands (value = reach and engagement on their content, directly reduced by this change), and Facebook (value = a platform users trust enough to keep using long-term). A raw time-spent or engagement North Star would have argued against this change entirely, since it explicitly traded away some of both; the change implies the company adopted something closer to a meaningful-interaction rate (comments, replies, shares to a specific person) as a more relevant proxy for long-term platform health, implementable from existing interaction-type event logs, guardrailed by overall session frequency (making sure the platform isn't abandoned outright) and by publisher/business page reach (an explicit, acknowledged cost to a distinct stakeholder that needed separate mitigation, like the Page-specific tools Facebook built afterward).

For a feed-ranking team making this kind of change, I'd set a goal on meaningful-interaction rate specifically, accepting a defined, bounded near-term decline in total time spent as an explicitly budgeted cost rather than a surprise, and I'd defend this to a revenue-focused stakeholder by presenting the trade-off transparently upfront (this will cost X in the short term, we expect Y in long-term retention and trust) rather than by hiding the near-term cost. I'd check a few quarters later whether session frequency and self-reported satisfaction actually improved, which would validate the bet, versus whether the platform simply lost the reduced engagement without a retention benefit, which would mean the trade-off wasn't actually worth its cost.

pitfalls: Refusing any near-term engagement decline on principle, missing that a deliberate, bounded trade-off can be the right long-term call
Not defining upfront what evidence, a few quarters later, would confirm or disconfirm that the trade-off actually paid off

cases.title: Weigh delivery speed against order accuracy for Zomato
cases.prompt: Zomato could push delivery partners and kitchens harder to reduce average delivery time, but faster handling can increase the rate of missing items or wrong orders. How would you think about this trade-off between delivery speed and order accuracy?
context: Zomato is a food delivery platform that displays an estimated delivery time to users before they order and tracks actual delivery time against that estimate.
Zomato allows users to report order issues including missing items and incorrect items through in-app support.
Zomato's restaurant partners are responsible for order preparation and packing before handoff to a delivery partner.
assumptions: assumed: faster kitchen preparation time and faster packing are correlated with a higher rate of packing errors, based on typical speed-accuracy trade-offs in manual fulfillment processes
assumed: both delivery time and order-issue reports are logged per order and attributable to a specific restaurant partner
followUps: How would you tell whether a specific restaurant's speed-up is causing more errors, versus another restaurant achieving the same speed without more errors?
How would you decide whether to intervene by restaurant, or by a platform-wide policy change?
What would make you accept a slightly slower delivery time platform-wide in exchange for fewer order issues?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume faster kitchen prep and packing correlates with more packing errors, and that both delivery time and issue reports are logged per order and attributable to a specific restaurant. Plan: frame why this is a genuine trade-off, not just a case for pushing speed everywhere, define the ecosystem and metrics, then propose a restaurant-level rather than platform-wide approach.

Zomato's competitiveness depends partly on delivery speed, since users comparing delivery apps often weight estimated time heavily, but a wrong or missing order is a much worse experience than a slightly slow one, since it directly fails the core promise of getting the food you ordered — an order-issue is likely to depress repeat usage more than a few extra minutes of wait would. This means pushing speed as a blanket policy risks trading a soft, forgivable cost (mild wait-time increase avoided) for a hard, unforgivable one (a meaningfully worse order-issue rate) at some restaurants.

Ecosystem players: the user (value = getting the correct order reasonably quickly), the restaurant partner (value = throughput without excessive error-driven refund cost), and Zomato (value = a platform users trust for both speed and accuracy). Since neither speed nor accuracy alone is a good sole North Star — pure speed ignores the accuracy cost identified above, and pure accuracy could justify unnecessarily slow handling — I'd propose a joint restaurant-level metric like 'on-time and accurate delivery rate' (both conditions met), implementable by joining existing delivery-time and issue-report logs at the order level, guardrailed by delivery time itself (so the accuracy focus doesn't silently let speed regress with no accountability) and issue-report rate specifically (an early, direct signal of the trade-off going wrong at a given restaurant). Any restaurant showing a rising issue rate alongside a speed push should be flagged for coaching or a slower target, rather than applying a platform-wide speed policy uniformly.

For the restaurant-operations team, I'd set a goal to raise the on-time-and-accurate delivery rate for a defined cohort of restaurants with currently below-average performance, rather than a blanket delivery-time reduction target, since that directly targets the joint metric rather than pushing one side of the trade-off in isolation. I'd keep issue-report rate as a hard guardrail specifically for any restaurant receiving speed-focused coaching, so an operational push doesn't quietly worsen the exact problem it's meant to avoid.

pitfalls: Pushing a platform-wide delivery-speed target without a restaurant-level accuracy guardrail, risking a rise in order issues at restaurants where the speed-accuracy trade-off is real
Treating delivery time and order accuracy as fully independent metrics instead of a joint outcome that should be measured and targeted together

cases.title: Set a quarterly goal for Spotify's Discover Weekly team
cases.prompt: Spotify's Discover Weekly is a personalized weekly playlist of recommended tracks, refreshed every Monday. As PM for the team owning it, what quarterly goal would you set, and how would you defend the number?
context: Spotify's Discover Weekly is a personalized playlist of 30 tracks, refreshed automatically every Monday for each user based on their listening history.
Spotify's business model includes both an ad-supported free tier and a paid Premium subscription.
Spotify has publicly discussed the role of personalized playlists like Discover Weekly in driving music discovery and engagement.
assumptions: assumed: 'save to library' and 'add to another playlist' actions on a track are logged and attributable back to its Discover Weekly origin
assumed: the team can influence the underlying recommendation model's tuning within a quarter, without needing a full model architecture change
followUps: If your goal is a save-rate lift, how would you make sure the team doesn't just recommend more familiar, lower-discovery tracks to inflate the number?
How would you defend this goal against a stakeholder who cares more about overall listening hours than about Discover Weekly specifically?
What would make you recommend a different goal than the one you just proposed?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume save and add-to-playlist actions on Discover Weekly tracks are logged and attributable to the playlist's origin, and that the team can meaningfully influence recommendation tuning within a quarter. Plan: frame the product and business context, define the ecosystem and metric logic, then propose and defend a specific team-level goal.

Spotify's core value proposition beyond a music library is helping users find things they wouldn't have found themselves, which is exactly what Discover Weekly is designed to do; its business model benefits from this both directly (differentiation from competitors with less personalization) and indirectly (more time spent, feeding both ad impressions and subscription retention). The mission connecting company strategy to this team specifically is 'make discovery feel as reliable and personal as a knowledgeable friend's recommendation.'

Ecosystem players are the listener (value = genuinely liking what's recommended), artists (value = discovery and streams from an audience that wouldn't have found them otherwise), and Spotify (value = engagement and differentiation). A company-level North Star here would be something like overall listening hours or retention, but that's too broad and lagging for a single feature team to own directly; the team needs an implementable, playlist-specific metric like save-to-library rate or add-to-other-playlist rate per Discover Weekly track, both trackable from existing event logs and both reasonable proxies for 'the recommendation was actually good,' distinct from a skip, which is a weaker and noisier signal.

For the Discover Weekly team, I'd set a goal on raising save-or-add rate per playlist by a defined percentage this quarter, since it's directly actionable through recommendation-model tuning and it's a stronger discovery signal than raw play-through or skip rate. I'd guardrail this against artist/genre diversity within the playlist (a proxy for genuine discovery rather than recommending only very familiar, high-save-probability tracks to game the number) and against overall listening-hours trend (confirming the tuning change doesn't quietly reduce total engagement even if save rate rises), defending the goal to a hours-focused stakeholder by showing that genuine discovery is a leading indicator of long-term retention, even if its immediate effect on total hours is small.

pitfalls: Setting a save-rate goal that can be gamed by recommending only safe, highly-familiar tracks, undermining the actual discovery purpose of the feature
Picking a company-wide metric like total listening hours as the team's own goal when it's too lagging and too far from what the team directly controls

cases.title: Set a quarterly goal for PhonePe's UPI reliability team
cases.prompt: PhonePe processes a large volume of UPI (Unified Payments Interface) transactions daily, where a failed or delayed transaction directly affects user trust. As PM for the team owning payment reliability, what quarterly goal would you set, and how would you defend the number?
context: PhonePe is a major UPI payments app in India, processing person-to-person and merchant transactions over the UPI network, which is operated by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India).

UPI transaction success depends on multiple parties in the chain: the paying app, the receiving app or merchant, the banks on both ends, and the NPCI switch itself, meaning a failure isn't always attributable to a single party.
PhonePe surfaces transaction status (success, pending, failed) to users within the app.
assumptions: assumed: transaction failures are attributable, via logging, to a specific stage in the chain (PhonePe's own system, the receiving bank, or the NPCI switch) with reasonable but imperfect accuracy
assumed: PhonePe's reliability team can directly control and improve its own system's failure rate, but can only partially influence bank-side or NPCI-side failures through escalation and retry logic
followUps: How would you set a goal that's fair given the team can't control bank-side or NPCI-side failures directly?
How would you defend prioritizing reliability investment over a growth or new-feature initiative competing for the same engineering resources?
What would make you escalate a specific bank's failure rate to NPCI rather than trying to solve it within PhonePe alone?

stages.walkthrough: I'll assume failures are attributable, with reasonable accuracy, to a specific stage in the multi-party UPI chain, and that PhonePe's team fully controls its own system's failure rate but only partially influences bank-side or NPCI-side failures. Plan: frame why reliability is strategically important here, define the ecosystem and metric logic, then propose a goal scoped to what the team actually controls.

PhonePe's entire value proposition is being a trusted, instant way to move money, and at UPI's transaction volume even a small failure rate translates into a large absolute number of frustrated users, some of whom may switch to a competing app after a bad experience. Because payments are often urgent (paying a vendor, splitting a bill in the moment), a failed or stuck transaction is a uniquely high-trust-cost failure mode compared to a typical app bug, which justifies treating reliability as a first-class, continuously-invested-in priority rather than a background maintenance concern.

Ecosystem players: the user (value = a transaction that reliably completes or fails fast and clearly, never gets stuck ambiguously), merchants (value = reliable settlement to keep accepting UPI), and PhonePe (value = trust that drives continued usage over competing apps). A single overall UPI-success-rate North Star would obscure the multi-party attribution problem, so I'd propose the team's core metric be 'PhonePe-attributable failure rate' — the share of failures traceable specifically to PhonePe's own systems, separate from bank- or NPCI-side failures, implementable via existing transaction-logging and failure-classification data.
